name: ctl
desc: Programming language for digital color management
why: A small programming language for color transforms in film and VFX pipelines, an odd domain with a real design of its own.

brief.what_it_is: CTL (Color Transformation Language) is a small domain-specific programming language for describing digital color transforms as programs. A color management system includes an interpreter that loads a CTL program and runs it on the pixels of an input image, producing a transformed output image. The command-line tool ctlrender applies a CTL transform to image files, for example ctlrender -ctl transform.ctl input.exr output.exr. Parameters such as exposure can be set to adjust a transform.
brief.why_it_exists: The README argues that general-purpose languages like C, C++ or Python are poor for sharing color transforms, because recipients may need to compile code, portability is hard to guarantee, bugs can crash a host application, and malware protection is difficult. CTL is restricted to the operations color transforms need, which the author says improves portability, protects host applications and users, and allows efficient interpreters.
brief.how_it_works: A color management system with CTL support runs an interpreter that loads a specific CTL program and applies it to the original image, which is the program's input, producing the transformed image as output. Two parties with the same CTL program and the same parameter settings get identical results, so transforms are shared by distributing the program. The language is limited to single-pixel operations, so it cannot express neighborhood operations such as blurs or whole-image statistics.

brief.install_notes: On macOS, brew install ctl is the recommended route and is said to pull in dependencies. Building from source is for Linux (Ubuntu/Debian/Red Hat) or custom macOS builds and needs a C++ compiler, CMake 3.12+, and OpenEXR; libTIFF and the ACES Container are optional. Windows builds use vcpkg with the CMake toolchain file, with openexr and tiff installed through vcpkg. Docker is offered as an isolated alternative, and host folders must be mounted to reach your files. No accounts or runtimes are mentioned beyond that.
brief.standout: CTL is a deliberately locked-down language: it can only express single-pixel color math, so transforms can be shared as plain program text with predictable results and no risk of arbitrary code running in a host application. That sandboxed-by-design stance is unusual for a scripting language, and the README is explicit that CTL is separate from ACES even though ACES uses it for its reference transforms.
brief.status: unknown. The README and the INSTALL.md I read show no release version, last-commit date, or maintenance note. The repo is hosted under the aces-aswf organization and includes CI workflows and Docker files, which suggests active upkeep, but I could not confirm recency from the pages.
brief.caveats: The language is restricted to color space and other single-pixel operations, so it cannot do blurs, sharpening, or whole-image statistics. Source builds take real work: a C++ compiler plus CMake, OpenEXR and optional libTIFF, and Windows needs vcpkg. Docker users must mount a host folder or they cannot reach their files. The README says the language is documented in SMPTE RDD 15 and in the repo docs. The INSTALL.md URL on the main branch returned 404 and I read the master-branch copy instead. The brew_caveats field was empty.
